title: The doctrine of God
for: I want to know who God is
subtitle: Ten sessions on who God is: whether he can be known, the name he gave Moses, what he is like, how he rules the world, and what the church means when it confesses him as Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
intro: Every life is shaped by what it takes God to be, whether it believes in him or not. A small god makes for anxious worship and easy unbelief; a true picture of God changes how a person prays, suffers, works and loves. These ten sessions ask who God is: whether he can be known at all, the name he gave at the burning bush, what he is like in himself and toward us, how he rules the world, and what the church means when it confesses one God in three persons.

The doctrine of God sits on the floor of the creeds. That there is one God, that he is the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and that he made all things is confessed plainly here, as the whole church confesses it. Where faithful Christians differ, over how God's rule fits human choice or whether God suffers, each view is set out in its strongest voice and left open. By the end you should be able to say who God is in your own words, show where Scripture teaches it, and explain the Trinity without reaching for an egg.

about: This guide is for anyone leading a small group through The doctrine of God. It suits Christians who want to know the God they worship more truly, and it suits the honest outsider who wants to hear what Christians actually mean by God before deciding whether to believe it. The leader's task is to keep the group in Scripture, to confess plainly what the creeds confess about the one God who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and to leave room where faithful Christians differ.

Each person reads the session, opens its page and does what it asks before the group meets. The meeting doesn't repeat the teaching. It talks over what people found, using the group guide for that session, gathered below in order with the page each session opens and the question it asks.

sections.title: The group
body: Four to ten people is a good size. Meet for about seventy-five minutes, once a week or once a fortnight, for ten meetings, and keep the end time you promised. The theology pages are long, so say at the start that no one needs to read every word, only enough to bring one thing they noticed. A leader doesn't need to be a theologian. A leader needs to have done the reading, to be at ease with mystery, and to be willing to say they don't know.

sections.title: The room
body: A table works best, with Bibles open in front of everyone, in print or on a phone, and paper for notes. Make it plain at the first meeting that anyone may pass on any question, that the group will disagree about some things and that this is allowed, and that no one has to pray aloud. What people say about their own lives stays in the room, unless someone is in danger.

sections.title: The order of a meeting
body: About seventy-five minutes, in this order. Keep to the times loosely and to the end time strictly.
steps: Ten minutes: the opening question, once round the circle. Anyone may pass.
Ten minutes: one person reads the verse aloud, and the passage around it, while the others follow.
Thirty-five minutes: the three questions to talk over, in order. Ask where each answer is found, in Scripture or on the page.
Ten minutes: what each person did with the session's task, and what it showed them about God.
Five minutes: the prayer prompt, in the group's own words.
Five minutes: name the next session and the page it opens, and say when you will meet.

sections.title: When a hard question comes
body: When a disputed question comes up, first ask what order it is. That there is one God, that the Father, the Son and the Spirit are each fully God, and that God is good and not the author of evil are first-order, and the sessions say so plainly. How God's rule fits human freedom, and whether God suffers, divide faithful theologians but not the faith, and the group should leave them open.

Let each view be stated in a form its own defenders would accept before anyone argues against it. When the group reaches the edge of what can be said about God, say so; that edge is part of the doctrine, not a failure of it. An outsider's honest objection is a gift to the group, and the errors in session 8 are to be named without mocking anyone who holds them.

sections.title: When someone is hurting
body: The doctrine of God lands on lives. A session on God as Father can land on someone whose own father was absent or cruel, and a session on providence can land on someone in the middle of a loss that no explanation reaches. When the study touches someone's life, stop and listen. Thank them for saying it, don't explain their suffering for them, and don't hurry back to the outline. Ask whether they would like the group to go on or to pause, and speak with them on their own afterwards.

If someone says that a partner, a leader or anyone else is harming them or a child, take it seriously and don't promise to keep it secret. A child who may be in danger is a matter for the authorities, not only for the group.

sections.title: When to point someone to Find Help
body: Point someone to Find Help when what they carry has become too heavy to set down: grief that has taken their sleep or appetite for weeks, fear or guilt that will not let them rest, harm done to them at home or in a church, or any sign that they no longer want to be alive. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and its lines for help right now are open day and night. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number. A leader is a friend in that moment, not a counsellor, and the kindest thing is often to stay with the person while they make the first call.

sessions.title: Can God be known?
teaching: Two things are true at once, and the doctrine of God begins by holding both. God is beyond us. He isn't one more thing in the universe, however large, and no mind can take his measure: “as the heavens are higher than the earth, so My ways are higher than your ways” (Isaiah 55:9). Theologians call this incomprehensibility. It doesn't mean God can't be understood at all. It means he can't be understood completely, the way a child can truly know her father without knowing everything about him.

And God can be known, because he has made himself known. The skeptic's question, how a finite mind could grasp an infinite God, is a fair one, and the Christian answer agrees with half of it: it couldn't, unaided. Scripture's claim is that God has come the other way. “No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, has made Him known” (John 1:18). To know God in the Bible's sense is more than holding correct facts about him. It is to be known by him and to know him in return, as persons know each other.

open.label: Who God is, in the Study Bible
open.why: The Study Bible's study of the one living God, above his creation and present to every part of it, traced through both testaments.

also.label: Why is there something rather than nothing?
also.why: The oldest argument from the world to God, with the strongest objections stated fairly, for what reason can reach and what it can't.

also.label: Why can't I see God?
also.why: A short film made for families on why God is unseen, and how he has made himself known, most of all in Jesus.

sessions.question: Is there a difference between knowing about God and knowing God, and which describes you now?
sessions.do: Read Jeremiah 9:23-24. Write down the three things the LORD says he delights in, and one thing that surprises you about what he wants to be known for.

verse.text: Now this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent.

group.open: When you were a child, what did you picture when you thought about God?
discuss: How can God be beyond our understanding and still truly known?
What does John 1:18 claim about how God is known, and why does it matter for a skeptic?
What is the difference between knowing facts about a person and knowing the person?
group.pray: Ask God to make himself known to each person in the group, and give thanks that he has come near in his Son.

sessions.title: The name God gave Moses
teaching: At the burning bush Moses asks the question every reader of the Bible eventually asks: who are you? God answers, “I AM WHO I AM” (Exodus 3:14). Then he gives the name itself, four Hebrew letters, YHWH, tied to the verb to be. Most English Bibles print it as the LORD in small capitals, following the old Jewish reverence that read Adonai, Lord, in place of the name. The name speaks of a God who simply is, who depends on nothing and no one, and who will be present with his people as he promised.

A name in Scripture tells you who someone is, and God fills his name with content when he passes before Moses on the mountain and proclaims it: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). Later Scripture returns to that sentence again and again, in the psalms, the prophets and the prayers of Israel. And in John's Gospel Jesus takes the words of the bush for himself: “before Abraham was born, I am” (John 8:58). His hearers understood him well enough to pick up stones.

open.label: Exodus 3, passage by passage
open.why: The burning bush and the giving of the divine name, read with notes on the Hebrew and on what the name promised Israel.

also.label: The names of God, in the Study Bible
also.why: Elohim, El Shaddai, Adonai, the LORD and the titles of the New Testament, each traced to where Scripture first gives it.

also.label: Follow a verse: cross-references
also.why: Start from Exodus 34:6 and follow its cross-references, to see how often later Scripture returns to the name God proclaimed to Moses.

sessions.question: What does it change to call God by the name he gave rather than by a title we chose for him?
sessions.do: Read Exodus 34:6-7, then find the same words again in Psalm 103:8, Jonah 4:2 and Joel 2:13. Note what each writer does with them.

verse.text: The LORD is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion.

group.open: What does your own name mean, and does it say anything true about you?
discuss: What does the name given at the bush tell Moses about God that a title like Almighty does not?
Why do so many later books repeat the words of Exodus 34:6?
What did Jesus' hearers understand him to claim in John 8:58, and why did they react as they did?
group.pray: Give thanks for the name of the LORD and for what he has said it means, and ask to know him by that name.

sessions.title: The God who needs nothing
teaching: Some of God's attributes belong to him alone; theologians call them incommunicable, because he doesn't share them with creatures. Aseity, from the Latin for from himself, means God exists of himself and needs nothing. Paul told the philosophers of Athens that God is not “served by human hands, as if He needed anything” (Acts 17:25). Immutability means he doesn't change in his being, character or purposes. Eternity means he has no beginning or end: “from everlasting to everlasting You are God” (Psalm 90:2). Omnipresence means no place is outside his presence, though he isn't spread thin through space like a gas.

These sound remote, but they are the ground of comfort. A God who needs nothing didn't make you to fill a lack in himself; he made you out of sheer generosity. A God who doesn't change will keep tomorrow the promise he made yesterday. Christians have argued over some of the details, such as whether God's unchangeableness means he cannot suffer, and the classical and passibilist views are each held by faithful theologians. The church agrees on the center: God is not a larger version of us, and he is not in need of anything we can give.

open.label: What are the attributes of God?
open.why: Classical theism and its more relational critics, each stated fairly, on God's self-existence, unchangeableness, eternity and presence everywhere.

also.label: Does God suffer?
also.why: Classical impassibility, the suffering God and the mediating view, set out as their own defenders would put them, with what all agree on named first.

also.label: Acts 17, passage by passage
also.why: Paul in Athens, telling philosophers about a God who made everything and needs nothing from anyone.

sessions.question: Which is harder for you to believe: that God needs nothing from you, or that he loves you anyway?
sessions.do: Read Psalm 90 aloud. Write down every line that sets God's eternity beside the shortness of a human life, and what the psalmist asks for because of it.

verse.text: Every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights, with whom there is no change or shifting shadow.

group.open: Who in your life has loved you without needing anything from you?
discuss: How does God's self-existence change the reason he made the world, and you?
Why is God's unchangeableness good news rather than coldness?
What is each side of the debate over whether God suffers trying to protect?
group.pray: Give thanks that God needs nothing and gives everything, and rest together in the God who does not change.

sessions.title: Holy, loving, just, wise and good
teaching: Other attributes God shares with his creatures in a creaturely measure: holiness, love, justice, wisdom and goodness. Theologians call them communicable. Holiness stands first in Isaiah's vision, called out three times by the seraphim: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory” (Isaiah 6:3). Holiness is God's set-apartness, his majesty and his moral purity together. Isaiah's first response wasn't admiration. He cried that he was ruined, a man of unclean lips, until a coal from the altar touched his mouth and his guilt was taken away.

God's attributes aren't parts, and they don't take turns. His love is a holy love and his justice a loving justice, and the cross is where both are seen whole. That matters because people tend to keep one. Some want a God of love who never judges, others a God of justice who is hard to love, and most of us drift toward whichever suits our side. Scripture won't let either stand: the same proclamation that calls the LORD compassionate and gracious says he “will by no means leave the guilty unpunished” (Exodus 34:7). His wisdom orders all things well, and his goodness gives to all.

open.label: Holiness, in the Study Bible
open.why: What it means that God is holy, and how a holy God makes a people able to live near him, from Sinai to the prophets.

also.label: Isaiah 6, passage by passage
also.why: The prophet's vision of the LORD high and lifted up, and the coal from the altar that took away his guilt.

also.label: Love, in the Study Bible
also.why: God's love and the love he commands, from the law of Moses to the letters of John, measured finally by the cross.

sessions.question: Which attribute of God do you find easiest to believe, and which do you quietly leave out?
sessions.do: Read Isaiah 6:1-8. Write down what Isaiah sees, what he confesses and what he says at the end, and note what happens between the second and the third.

verse.text: And they were calling out to one another: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory.”

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What word would you have used to describe God when you were twelve?
discuss: Why does Isaiah's vision of holiness lead first to confession rather than admiration?
Where do you see churches keeping God's love without his justice, or his justice without his love?
How does the cross show God's love and his justice at once?
group.pray: Confess together the ways the group has made God smaller than he is, and give thanks for the mercy that cleanses.

sessions.title: Sovereignty and providence
teaching: Scripture says plainly that God rules: “Our God is in heaven; He does as He pleases” (Psalm 115:3). Providence is that rule worked out day by day. God keeps the world in being, works in and through what happens in it, and directs it toward his ends. Rain and harvest, the rise of kings and the plans of ordinary people fall within it. And Scripture says just as plainly that human beings make real choices and answer for them. Joseph tells the brothers who sold him, “what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good” (Genesis 50:20). One event, two intentions, and both are real.

How those two truths fit is one of the church's oldest arguments. Compatibilists, many of them in the Reformed tradition, hold that God's decree and human freedom fit together because freedom means acting on your own desires without compulsion. Others, many Arminians among them, hold that freedom means the power to choose otherwise, and that God's rule makes room for it. Molinists propose that God knows what every free creature would do in every circumstance. All of them confess that God rules, that people are responsible, and that God is not the author of evil. That is the shared ground; the rest is room for faithful Christians to disagree.

open.label: Providence, in the Study Bible
open.why: God's continuing care and government of the world, from rain and harvest to the rise of kings, traced through Scripture.

also.label: Sovereignty and human freedom
also.why: Compatibilism, libertarian freedom and Molinism, each stated in the form its defenders would sign, with the ground they share named first.

also.label: Does God Have a Plan for My Life?
also.why: An essay on what providence promises, and what it does not promise, about the shape of a single life.

sessions.question: Where in your own life can you see, looking back, a hand you couldn't see at the time?
sessions.do: Read Genesis 50:15-21. Write down what Joseph says about his brothers' intention, what he says about God's, and what he then does for the brothers.

verse.text: A man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps.

care: If you are suffering now, for your faith or for any other reason, you do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Do you tend to think of your life as mostly chance, mostly plan, or something else?
discuss: What two things does Genesis 50:20 hold together, and why does it need both?
What is each view on the theology page trying to protect?
How can belief in providence comfort someone without explaining their suffering away?
group.pray: Give thanks for God's care over the group's ordinary days, and pray for anyone carrying something whose purpose they cannot yet see.

sessions.title: The Trinity in Scripture
teaching: The word Trinity isn't in the Bible, but the pattern it names runs all through it, and three strands have to be held together. First, there is one God. Israel's confession is “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One” (Deuteronomy 6:4), and the apostles never loosened it. Second, the Father is God, the Son is God and the Spirit is God: “the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1), and Peter tells Ananias that lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God. Third, the three are distinct. At Jesus' baptism the Father speaks from heaven, the Son stands in the water and the Spirit descends.

The New Testament writers didn't argue their way toward the Trinity; they lived inside it. Jesus sends his disciples to baptize “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19), one name and three persons. Paul ends a letter with the grace of the Lord Jesus, the love of God and the fellowship of the Spirit without stopping to explain. Many scholars read 1 Corinthians 8:6 as Paul taking the words of the Shema and placing Jesus inside them. The doctrine came later. The worship came first.

open.label: What is the Trinity?
open.why: The site's full treatment of one God in three persons from both testaments, with the one live evangelical debate, over eternal subordination, set out fairly.

also.label: Matthew 28, passage by passage
also.why: The risen Jesus sends his disciples to baptize in the one name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

also.label: Who God is: Father, Son and Holy Spirit
also.why: A short film in eight pictures on what the Bible shows about the one God, and why every other picture breaks.

sessions.question: Which of the three strands, one God, three who are God, three who are distinct, would you find hardest to show from Scripture?
sessions.do: Read Matthew 3:13-17. Write down what each of the three persons does in the scene, and what would be lost if any one of them were left out.

verse.text: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you.

group.open: When you hear the word Trinity, what comes to mind first?
discuss: Why does the church insist on all three strands at once?
What does it mean that the first disciples worshiped Jesus while still confessing the Shema?
Why might it matter that the worship came before the doctrine?
group.pray: Give thanks to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit, for making himself known as he is.

sessions.title: The Trinity in the church's creeds
teaching: Around 318 a presbyter in Alexandria named Arius taught that the Son was the first and greatest of God's creatures, so that there was a time when he did not exist. Arius was a serious man who believed he was protecting God's oneness. The Council of Nicaea in 325 answered that the Son is begotten, not made, of one being with the Father, using the Greek word homoousios. The word isn't in Scripture, and its critics said so. Its defenders, Athanasius above all, replied that if the Son is a creature, the church has been worshiping a creature, and a creature cannot save.

The argument went on for decades, and Athanasius was exiled five times for his part in it. The Council of Constantinople in 381 reaffirmed Nicaea and filled out what the creed says of the Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son. With one later Western addition that East and West still dispute, that is the Nicene Creed churches confess today. The Athanasian Creed, a Latin statement from the fifth or sixth century not written by Athanasius, sets the balance in careful lines: the persons are not confused, and the one being is not divided.

open.label: The Nicene Creed
open.why: The creed of 325 as completed in 381, with notes on the errors each line was written against and the one disputed addition.

also.label: Nicaea to Chalcedon: the councils that wrote the creeds
also.why: The church history lesson on the councils that wrote the creeds, with the people, the arguments and what it cost them.

also.label: The Athanasian Creed
also.why: The Western statement that sets out the Trinity in balanced lines, with notes on its origin and its hardest clauses.

also.label: What Was Decided at the Council of Nicaea?
also.why: An essay on what the council actually settled in 325, and the popular stories about it that the record doesn't support.

sessions.question: Why might the church need a word Scripture doesn't use in order to protect what Scripture says?
sessions.do: Read the Nicene Creed slowly. Underline every phrase about the Son, then every phrase about the Spirit, and next to each write one verse it seems to rest on.

verse.text: yet for us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist. And there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we exist.

group.open: Have you ever said the Nicene Creed in church, and what did it mean to you then?
discuss: What was Arius trying to protect, and why did the church still refuse his answer?
Why did Athanasius think the Son's full deity mattered for salvation itself?
What did the council of 381 add about the Spirit, and why was it needed?
group.pray: Give thanks for those who paid a price to keep the church's confession whole, and ask to confess it with understanding.

sessions.title: The errors the church refused
teaching: Every error about the Trinity begins as an attempt to make God easier to understand, and most were taught by sincere people. Modalism, linked with Sabellius in the third century, said the one God appears first as Father, then as Son, then as Spirit, like one actor in three masks. It keeps God's oneness and loses the persons: it can't explain the Son praying to the Father, or the Father speaking from heaven over the Son. Arianism keeps the Father's uniqueness and makes the Son a creature, which leaves salvation in the hands of someone who is not God.

Tritheism runs the other way, three gods in perfect agreement, which honors the persons and denies the Shema. The church refused each because each, in the end, changes the gospel. If the Son is a mask, the Father did not send him; if he is a creature, God did not come; if there are three gods, Christians worship more than one. Naming these errors isn't mockery of the people who held them. Their questions were good ones. And most Christians, asked to explain the Trinity on the spot, slide into one of them without meaning to. That includes the people who wrote this track.

open.label: The Trinity, in the Study Bible
open.why: Its sections on history and on errors trace modalism, Arianism, adoptionism and tritheism, and why the church refused each one.

also.label: How did Jesus become God?
also.why: The argument that the church turned a Jewish preacher into God over time, stated at full strength and weighed against the earliest sources.

also.label: The glossary
also.why: Short definitions of homoousios, hypostasis, perichoresis, aseity and the other technical words, for when the terms begin to blur.

sessions.question: Which of these errors do you think you would have found most persuasive, and why?
sessions.do: Read John 17:1-5. Write down how Jesus speaks to the Father, and which of the three errors each verse would make hard to hold.

verse.text: And now, Father, glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed.

group.open: Which explanation of the Trinity did you first hear, and was it one of these errors?
discuss: What does each error get right, and what does it give up?
How does each error change the gospel, not only the doctrine?
How can a group name an error plainly without mocking the people who hold it?
group.pray: Pray for those who have been taught a smaller God, and for the group to speak of God truly and with love.

sessions.title: The Trinity in prayer and life
teaching: The Trinity isn't a puzzle set beside the Christian life. It is the shape of it. Christians pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit, and Paul puts it in one line: “For through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit” (Ephesians 2:18). Because the Son has made believers children of God, the Spirit of the Son in them calls God Father, as Paul tells the Galatians. Prayer is not a lonely voice sent into the dark. It is a child brought by the Son to the Father, with the Spirit's help for the words.

It shapes more than prayer. Before the world existed, the Father, the Son and the Spirit lived in love; God didn't become loving when he made someone to love. So love isn't something human beings invented to get along. It is older than the universe. The church is meant to be a small picture of that life: many persons, one body, no one swallowed and no one left alone. A church that is only a crowd, or only a chain of command, has forgotten whose image it bears, and most of us have belonged to both.

open.label: Romans 8, passage by passage
open.why: Paul's chapter on life in the Spirit, where the Spirit of adoption teaches believers to call God Father and helps them pray.

also.label: Prayer
also.why: A short film in seven pictures on what prayer is, talking with God as Father, and what to do when an answer is slow to come.

also.label: How to pray when you don't feel like it
also.why: Practical help for the mornings when prayer feels empty, for anyone who wants this session to reach an ordinary day.

also.label: What are the one another commands?
also.why: The New Testament's commands to love, bear, confess and forgive one another, the life of a church that reflects the God it worships.

sessions.question: When you pray, whom do you picture yourself speaking to, and how might praying to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit change it?
sessions.do: For three days, begin your prayer by naming each person: thanking the Father, coming through the Son, asking for the Spirit's help. On the third day write down what changed, if anything.

verse.text: For through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit.

group.open: What does your prayer usually sound like when no one else is listening?
discuss: What does Ephesians 2:18 say each person of the Trinity does in prayer?
If love is older than creation, what does that change about the way we love?
Where is our own church more like a crowd or a chain of command than a body?
group.pray: Pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit, asking that the group's life together would show the love God has always had.

sessions.title: Explaining the Trinity simply
teaching: Most analogies for the Trinity end in one of the errors. Water as ice, liquid and steam is one thing in three forms, which is modalism. An egg's shell, white and yolk makes each person a third of God. A man who is a father, a son and a husband is one person in three roles. The church's restraint here is wisdom rather than timidity. No created thing is a full picture of the Creator, and admitting that is part of explaining him truly.

So say it plainly. There is one God. The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God. They are not each other, and they are not three gods. A child can hold those sentences, and a theologian never gets to the bottom of them. Then say why it matters. If the Son is God, then God himself came to rescue us. If the Spirit is God, then God himself lives in those who trust him. The mystery isn't a contradiction. It is what it looks like to meet a God larger than our categories, who has still made himself known.

open.label: How can God be three and one?
open.why: The Honest Answer for the person who thinks the Trinity is a contradiction, which takes the charge seriously before it answers.

also.label: How to answer hard questions about God
also.why: Practical counsel for answering a child's questions about God honestly, including the ones a parent can't fully answer.

also.label: Who is God? The Trinity
also.why: The site's treatment of God and the Trinity together, for anyone who wants the plain sentences of this session tested at greater depth.

also.label: The tracks
also.why: Next in Theology in Depth: The person and work of Christ, on who Jesus is and what he has done, following the Son into the world.

sessions.question: How would you explain the Trinity to a ten-year-old in five sentences, without an analogy?
sessions.do: Write your five sentences. Then test each one against the three errors from session 8, and rewrite any sentence that slides into one of them.

verse.text: O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways!

group.open: What is the worst explanation of the Trinity you have ever heard?
discuss: Which common analogy have you used, and which error does it slide into?
Why is it wisdom, not weakness, to say no created thing fully pictures God?
How would you explain why the Trinity matters, not only what it is?
group.pray: Give thanks for the one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and ask for clear and humble words when someone asks who he is.
